summary: Explains how to use packet delay variation metrics, which appear in many standards. The metric in RFC 3393 is very flexible, so this document guides which formulation to pick for particular uses and discusses how results should be interpreted.

plainLanguage.summary: Packet delay variation measures how much packet travel times differ. RFC 5481 compares two ways to calculate it and explains which is more useful for tasks such as sizing a de-jitter buffer, comparing service levels, or analyzing changes in a path.

questions: what is the difference between ipdv and pdv
which delay variation measure helps size a buffer
subtitle: Guidance for choosing between two packet delay variation measurements and interpreting their results.

tldr.problem: The RFC 3393 delay-variation metric allows multiple packet-selection methods, which can make measurement results difficult to compare.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5481 compares IPDV, which references the previous packet, with PDV, which references the packet with minimum delay in the sample.
tldr.outcome: PDV directly supports buffer sizing, queue analysis, composition, and simple service-level summaries. IPDV can be useful with clock skew or for some short-term changes.

today: RFC 5481 is Informational and was published in March 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Ways to Measure Delay Variation
sections.content:
Delay variation compares one-way delay measurements for packets in a stream. The RFC focuses on two formulations allowed by RFC 3393. IPDV compares each packet with the previous packet in sending order; PDV compares each packet with a reference, usually the packet with minimum delay in the sample.

IPDV values may be positive, negative, or zero. PDV values are zero or positive because the reference is the minimum. The two distributions answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable.
sections.plainLanguage: IPDV compares each packet's delay with the previous packet's delay. PDV compares each packet with the lowest delay in the sample.

sections.title: What the Measurements Show
sections.content:
PDV shifts the one-way-delay distribution so its minimum is zero. Its range or a high percentile can indicate the delay variation that a de-jitter buffer needs to accommodate. When the sample minimum is the true minimum path delay, the PDV distribution corresponds to the queueing-time distribution experienced by the test stream.

IPDV measures changes between consecutive delays and can distinguish short-term changes from longer trends. Its mean is usually zero unless a long-term delay trend or clock-frequency error is present. Unlike PDV, IPDV results depend on packet sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: PDV shows how far packet delays extend above the sample minimum, which helps estimate a buffer range. IPDV shows changes from one packet to the next.

sections.title: When Each Form Is Useful
sections.content:
The RFC favors PDV for de-jitter buffer sizing, estimating queue occupation, spatial composition, and service-level specifications that report one number. Its one-sided distribution can be summarized with a percentile or range. Validated spatial-composition methods described in the RFC use PDV.

IPDV can be useful when measurement clocks have appreciable skew because it compares nearby packet delays. It may also help separate effects around path changes. However, when a path change occurs with packet loss, IPDV may not show it if no consecutive received packets span the change. PDV can retain results for arriving packets and may show multiple delay modes.
sections.plainLanguage: PDV is suited to buffer sizing and clear service-level summaries. IPDV can help when clock skew matters, but packet loss can hide some path changes from it.

sections.title: Measurement Choices Affect Results
sections.content:
Both forms depend on the one-way-delay measurements and the test stream. The RFC discusses Poisson and periodic sampling; periodic streams are often used when the measurement should reflect applications with regular packet spacing. Measurement duration should be similar to the user session being studied, and short intervals can reduce the effect of path changes and clock skew.

Devices with limited storage may need to choose statistics in advance. To calculate useful PDV summaries later, a device can retain the minimum delay and several of the largest delays rather than every measurement. The RFC also discusses clock synchronization, packet loss, reordering, and separating samples when paths change.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet stream, measurement duration, clocks, and storage limits affect results. Choose a measurement period that matches the session or service being evaluated.
